We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & {\alpha }_{1}t \\ -2{\alpha }_{1}t & 2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=0,\,{\lambda }_{2}=t,
$$

both of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}r(0)={e}^{0} \\ r(t)={e}^{t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0}=1 \\ t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the first equation, we immediately get

$$
{\alpha }_{0}=1.
$$

- Substituting ${\alpha }_{0}=1$ into the second equation, we get

$$
t{\alpha }_{1}+1={e}^{t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{1}=\frac{1}{t}({e}^{t}-1).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =-(\frac{1}{t}({e}^{t}-1))t+1 \\  & =-({e}^{t}-1)+1 \\  & =-{e}^{t}+2 \\ {\alpha }_{1}t & =(\frac{1}{t}({e}^{t}-1))t \\  & ={e}^{t}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{t}+2 & {e}^{t}-1 \\ 2-2{e}^{t} & 2{e}^{t}-1\end{aligned}].
$$
